title: APR, APY, and the 'More Users' Effect
objectives: Tell fee income apart from reward-token emissions
See why a 10,000% launch APR collapses the moment money arrives
Calculate real APY with compounding instead of trusting a dashboard number

steps.title: Why 10,000% APY is a Trap
steps.body:
Picture an ice-cream stand that gives away 100 free scoops a day. Five customers get stuffed. Five hundred customers get a lick each. A farm's advertised yield behaves exactly the same way.

When a protocol launches it quotes an enormous number — sometimes five figures — because it is splitting a fixed daily bucket of freshly printed tokens across a tiny pile of early deposits. Those printed tokens are <Term id="emissions">emissions</Term>, and the pile they are split across is the pool's <Term id="tvl">TVL</Term>.

With $1,000 in the pool, each dollar claims a fat slice of the bucket, so the annualised <Term id="apr">APR</Term> looks absurd. Add $100,000 and the same bucket is shared a hundred ways more.

The trap in one sentence: that huge number is not a forecast of profit. It is a photograph of how few people were there before you showed up.

steps.title: The 'More Users' Dilution Effect
steps.body:
The tour bus pulls up. Word spreads and 100 new depositors put in $1,000 each. TVL jumps from $1,000 to $101,000. The daily emissions bucket has not changed by a single token.

Same pie, a hundred more mouths:

- The fixed drip is now spread across roughly 100 times more capital.
- The quoted APR collapses from five figures toward something ordinary, and keeps sliding with every deposit.
- Your principal did not shrink. The rate you were shown evaporated because the denominator exploded.

This is not a bug and it is not a scam. It is arithmetic, and it is guaranteed. The question to ask about any <Term id="apr">APR</Term> is always the same: how big is the pool right now, and how fast is it filling?

Two checks worth running before you deposit anything:

- Compare today's rate with last week's. If it fell off a cliff, you are probably late.
- A falling APR is not automatically bad. A large, steady pool paying a modest rate routinely beats a tiny pool paying a fantasy one.

steps.title: Under the Hood: Per-Share Reward Accounting
steps.body:
A farm contract cannot loop over thousands of wallets every few seconds — that would burn a fortune in fees on every update. Instead it uses per-share accounting, and the core update is one line:

`accumulatedRewardPerShare += (dailyEmissions × deltaTime) / totalStaked`

How it works:

- The contract keeps one running number: rewards owed per staked unit.
- When you deposit, it snapshots that number as your `rewardDebt`.
- When you claim, your payout is `yourShare × accumulatedRewardPerShare − yourRewardDebt`.

One cheap multiplication per user instead of touching everyone. It also explains dilution precisely: `totalStaked` sits in the denominator, so every new deposit shrinks the increment and lowers everyone's future per-share rewards in real time. No admin has to press a button.

One detail worth keeping: the denominator is measured in staked dollars, not in wallets. A single whale adding $1M dilutes you exactly as much as a thousand users adding $1,000 each. Dollars dilute, headcount does not — and the compounding of that per-share drip is the difference between the quoted <Term id="apr">APR</Term> and the <Term id="apy">APY</Term> you actually keep.

questions.prompt: A farm hands out 1,000 reward tokens every single day no matter what. Total deposits grow from $10,000 to $100,000. What happens to the reward APR earned per dollar?
options: It rises roughly 10x, since the pool now holds far more value to earn against
It stays exactly the same, because the daily token drip never changes
It falls to roughly one-tenth (about a 90% drop), because the same rewards now spread over 10x the capital
It turns negative, because the contract claws back rewards already earned
questions.explainRight: Rewards per dollar equal fixed emissions divided by total capital. Multiply the denominator by ten and each dollar's share drops by ten. That inverse relationship is the single most useful instinct for reading any farm APR.
questions.explainWrong: Rewards are not paid per pool, they are paid per dollar of capital. Ten times the TVL with unchanged emissions means each dollar receives roughly a tenth of what it used to. Nothing is clawed back — the yield is simply sliced thinner.

questions.prompt: APR and APY both describe annual returns. What is the key difference between them?
options: APR includes the effect of compounding, while APY is the simple non-compounded rate
APR is the simple annual rate; APY folds in reinvesting your earnings so they compound on top of each other
APR applies only to lending pools, while APY applies only to liquidity pools
APY is always lower than APR, because it subtracts protocol fees before reporting
questions.explainRight: APR is a flat rate that ignores reinvestment. APY assumes your earnings are put back to work and start earning on their own. Frequent compounding is why an APY always sits above the matching APR.
questions.explainWrong: It is the other way around. APR is the simple rate and APY includes compounding, so the APY is the higher figure. If you never claim and restake, your real result will look closer to APR.

questions.prompt: A brand-new pool advertises 10,000% APY on day one. Which explanation best describes where that number comes from?
options: A guaranteed promotional payout the protocol is obliged to keep paying for a full year
An oracle reporting the future price appreciation of the reward token in advance
The protocol minting extra tokens only for the very first depositor as a loyalty bonus
A fixed daily emission drip divided by a tiny amount of early TVL, so each dollar looks enormously productive
questions.explainRight: Fixed emissions over a nearly empty pool. The moment capital arrives, the same bucket is split more ways and the rate collapses. The number describes how empty the pool is, not a durable income stream.
questions.explainWrong: No protocol can commit a year of five-figure yields out of thin air, and no oracle forecasts token prices. The figure is pure arithmetic — treat a launch APR as a snapshot of how few depositors exist, never as a promise.

questions.prompt: A pool pays out $1,000 of rewards per day. On Monday its TVL is $500,000. By Friday, new deposits push TVL to $2,000,000 while the daily reward is still $1,000. Roughly how does Friday's per-dollar APR compare with Monday's?
options: It is about 4x higher on Friday
It is about the same, since the daily reward amount never changed
It is about one-quarter of Monday's, because the same reward now spreads across 4x the TVL
It is about double, because extra TVL generates extra fee income
questions.explainRight: TVL quadrupled while the reward stayed flat, so every dollar now receives a quarter of its previous share. A fixed numerator and a 4x denominator is a 75% cut in per-dollar APR.
questions.explainWrong: The reward amount is constant, so the only thing that moved is how many dollars compete for it. Going from $500k to $2M divides each dollar's yield by four. Extra TVL does not create extra emissions; it only splits the existing flow more ways.

questions.prompt: Per-share reward accounting tracks a running `accumulatedRewardPerShare` and a per-user `rewardDebt`. What is `rewardDebt` for?
options: It snapshots the accumulated-reward-per-share value at deposit time, so a user only claims rewards earned after they joined
It records how much the user owes the protocol in gas fees for every claim
It freezes the user's principal so they cannot withdraw until emissions end
It tracks how little the user deposited, lowering their share of the pool
questions.explainRight: `rewardDebt` is a checkpoint taken at your deposit. Subtracting it from the current counter means you only collect rewards that accrued during your stay. That is what lets the contract pay everyone correctly with one multiplication per claim.
questions.explainWrong: It is not a real debt and not a lock. It is an accounting bookmark that excludes rewards generated before you arrived — without it, a late depositor could instantly claim the earlier crowd's earnings.

questions.prompt: A pool's advertised APR falls from 8,000% to 300% over two weeks, yet the emission schedule was never changed. What most likely happened?
options: The protocol secretly cut emissions by about 96%
TVL grew sharply as more capital piled in, diluting each dollar's slice of the same reward stream
The pool took impermanent loss, which mechanically lowers APR by definition
The reward token's price fell, even though TVL stayed perfectly flat
questions.explainRight: If emissions never changed, the numerator never shrank — so the collapse has to come from the denominator. A rush of new capital is the usual culprit, and it is the 'more users' effect in its natural habitat.
questions.explainWrong: Surging TVL dilutes each dollar's yield exactly like this. Impermanent loss affects the value of your position, not the advertised reward rate, and a flat TVL could not produce this collapse on its own.

questions.prompt: A pool quotes 100% APR paid continuously and auto-compounded. A friend concludes, 'so I roughly double my money in a year.' Using the APR/APY distinction, which reply is most accurate?
options: No - if the 100% compounds more often than once a year, APY climbs above 100%, so you would finish slightly above 2x
Correct - a 100% APR always means exactly 2x after one year, no matter the compounding
No - APY is always smaller than APR, so you would finish below 2x
Correct, but only if the reward token's price stays perfectly stable
questions.explainRight: Compounding adds return on top of return, so a 100% APR that is routinely reinvested lands above 100% APY. The more often it compounds, the further the final multiple overshoots a simple double.
questions.explainWrong: APR ignores compounding, so a reinvested 100% APR grows faster than a flat 2x. APY sits above 100%, not below. Whether the reward token holds its price is a separate risk that changes your dollar value, not the arithmetic.
